extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology/psychoanalysis, humor theorists, and researchers studying the mechanisms and production of jokes and the comic
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Freud's psychoanalytic criteria for understanding, evaluating, and producing jokes and comic effects — focusing on mechanisms like displacement, ambiguity, unconscious formation, social intelligibility, and the naïve. Useful for theoretical analysis or informing joke construction sensitive to audience and inhibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displacement and indirect representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Among displacements are to be counted not merely diversions from a train of thought but every sort of indirect representation as well, and in particular the replacement of an important but objectionable element by one that is indifferent and that appears innocent to the censorship, something that seems like a very remote allusion to the other one - substitution by a piece of symbolism, or an analogy, or something small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Displacements are used as joke-techniques but 'usually respect the limits imposed on their employment in conscious thinking' and are far less comprehensive than in dreams. They may be absent in many jokes but are especially valuable for tendentious jokes where they help overcome objections to a joke's purpose. Examples: indirect allusions, symbolism, small substitutions; useful when direct mention would trigger censorship or objection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity / double-sidedness ('sense in nonsense')
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing distinguishes jokes more clearly from all other psychical structures than this double-sidedness and this duplicity in speech. From this point of view ... authorities come closest to an understanding of the nature of jokes when they lay stress on 'sense in nonsense'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A joke should exploit the ambiguity and multiplicity of conceptual relations so that play or nonsense can at the same time appear allowable or sensible. Selecting occasions where a nonsensical utterance can be read as sensible (because of ambiguity) is central to producing a successful joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain play with words/unaltered nonsense rather than compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes do not, like dreams, create compromises; they do not evade the inhibition, but they insist on maintaining play with words or with nonsense unaltered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than disguising the play, a joke should preserve the verbal play or nonsense intact while choosing contexts in which it can pass scrutiny (e.g., because of ambiguity). The technique is to find occasions where the play appears allowable to conscious criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of allusion/displacement to serve tendentious aims
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest stage of jokes, tendentious jokes, often have to overcome two kinds of inhibition, those opposed to the joke itself and those opposed to its purpose ..., and that allusions and displacements are well qualified to make this latter task possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a joke carries an aggressive, political, sexual, or otherwise tendentious purpose, rely on indirect representation (allusion, displacement) to bypass both the general inhibition against joking and objections to the joke's intended purpose. Allusion lets the purpose be communicated while shielding the producer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by the opposite and irony
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation by the opposite is one of the more effective methods employed in jokes ... I am thinking of irony, which comes very close to joking ... Its essence lies in saying the opposite of what one intends to convey ... by one’s tone of voice, by some accompanying gesture, or (where writing is concerned) by some small stylistic indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony (saying the opposite) is a powerful device but depends on the audience being prepared to hear the opposite; it requires paralinguistic or stylistic cues to signal the intended contrary meaning and is particularly liable to be misunderstood if those cues are absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonsense/absurdity as intentional representational device
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonsense, absurdity, which appears so often in dreams ... can always be shown to have been admitted by the dream-work intentionally and to be designed to represent embittered criticism and contemptuous contradiction in the dream-thoughts. ... We have now learned ... that nonsense in jokes is made to serve the same aims of representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nonsense deliberately to represent criticism, contradiction, or to increase the hearer’s psychical expenditure and thus the quota liberated for discharge by laughing. The nonsense in a joke can also be an end in itself (recovering pleasure in nonsense). Distinguish this from comic forms (caricature, parody) that may not require the same unconscious processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unconscious selection of pleasurable wording
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to enable this thought to be turned into a joke, it is clearly necessary to select from among the possible forms of expression the precise one which brings along with it a yield of verbal pleasure. We know from self-observation that this selection is not made by conscious attention; ... an unconscious cathexis offers far more favourable conditions for selecting the expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective jokes often arise when selection of wording that yields verbal pleasure occurs below conscious control — the associative paths available in the unconscious facilitate finding puns, double meanings or formulations that produce verbal pleasure. Expect serendipity and aptitude rather than deliberate algorithmic construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of mood and personal aptitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The jest springs from a cheerful mood, which seems to be characterized by an inclination to diminish mental cathexes. ... In the case of innocent jokes and of jests, ... we must presume the occurrence of a special personal aptitude, which is manifested in the ease with which the preconscious cathexis is dropped ... Lastly, the joke-work receives its most powerful stimulus when strong purposes reaching down into the unconscious are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the creator's mood (cheerfulness facilitates jests) and individual aptitude (some people can make jokes independent of mood). Strong unconscious motives can powerfully stimulate joke production even in those otherwise inept at joking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social requirement and the binding condition of intelligibility (role of the third person)
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke, on the other hand, is the most social of all the mental functions that aim at a yield of pleasure. It often calls for three persons and its completion requires the participation of someone else in the mental process it starts. The condition of intelligibility is, therefore, binding on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that the joke can be 'completed' by the audience (the third person). Jokes must be intelligible to others; crafting a joke requires anticipating whether the listener(s) can reconstruct the intended double-meaning or relief mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit unconscious distortion to what the audience can 'set straight'
rubrics_metrics.description: A joke ... may only make use of possible distortion in the unconscious through condensation and displacement up to the point at which it can be set straight by the third person’s understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques borrowed from unconscious processes (condensation, displacement) are permissible in jokes only insofar as the audience can parse and repair them. Excessive distortion (as in dreams) will make the material unintelligible and fail as a joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'found' comic (naïve) and 'made' joke
rubrics_metrics.description: The type of the comic which stands nearest to jokes is the naïve. Like the comic in general, the naïve is 'found' and not, like a joke, 'made'. Indeed, the naïve cannot be made at all, whereas alongside the pure comic we have to take into account the case in which something is made comic - an evocation of the comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing humor, determine whether the comic is being produced (crafted) or discovered in another's behavior or speech. Naïve/comic effects arising from others' unselfconscious remarks require different interpretive criteria than deliberately constructed jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naïve effect requires perceived absence of inhibition in producer
rubrics_metrics.description: The naïve occurs if someone completely disregards an inhibition because it is not present in him ... It is a condition for the naïve’s producing its effect that we should know that the person concerned does not possess the inhibition; otherwise we call him not naïve but impudent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a naïve utterance to elicit laughter rather than indignation, listeners must be able to infer the speaker's innocence/ignorance. The audience's knowledge of the producer's psychological state is central to whether the remark reads as comically naïve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared inhibitions between speaker and audience for joke effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas it was a condition for the effectiveness of a joke that both persons should be subject to approximately the same inhibitions or internal resistances, it will be seen that it is a condition for the naïve that the one person should possess inhibitions which the other is without.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective jokes presuppose a common set of inhibitions or norms between producer and receiver; the humor often comes from temporarily lifting or economizing the inhibitory expenditure that both share. Mismatch in inhibitions changes the mechanism (leading to naïve or indignant responses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual source of comic pleasure: verbal yield plus economy in inhibition
rubrics_metrics.description: The pleasure from jokes has the same origin - a core of verbal pleasure and pleasure from nonsense, and a casing of pleasure in the lifting of inhibitions or in the relief of psychical expenditure ... In the naïve ... our pleasure in what we hear receives an increase ... in making this comparison we see ... we can economize the expenditure on keeping up this barrier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting or assessing humor, check for both: (1) a direct verbal/linguistic pleasure (puns, nonsense, wordplay) and (2) a secondary pleasure from lifting an inhibition or economizing psychical expenditure (relief). Both together often create the full comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathy/comparison mechanism producing comic pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: We take the producing person’s psychical state into consideration, put ourselves into it and try to understand it by comparing it with our own. It is these processes of empathy and comparison that result in the economy in expenditure which we discharge by laughing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic pleasure (especially in naïve examples) often arises when listeners mentally simulate the producer's state and compare it with their own, thereby economizing inhibitory effort. Encourage situations where the audience can easily imagine the speaker's perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of misunderstanding and the need for cues
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony can only be employed when the other person is prepared to hear the opposite, so that he cannot fail to feel an inclination to contradict. As a result of this condition, irony is exposed particularly easily to the danger of being misunderstood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear cues—tone, gesture, stylistic markers—especially in written or ambiguous contexts, to reduce misinterpretation. Evaluate whether an audience is 'prepared' to hear the intended opposite meaning before using irony or contradiction-as-joke.
